stories.title: Vaishnav's School Firecracker Prank
stories.description: Ajay recounts a story from his friend Vaishnav about a schoolboy who devised a delayed firecracker system on multiple floors of his school. By timing the explosions, he made the teachers run frantically from floor to floor. Ajay uses this to illustrate the latent innovation and potential in India's youth.

stories.title: The Stolen Bridge in Bihar
stories.description: Amit mentions a bizarre news story where an entire bridge was stolen in Bihar. The thieves even managed to steal the river path (metaphorically or literally diverting it). This highlights the 'insane' level of innovation, albeit criminal, present in India.

stories.title: Origin of I18N
stories.description: Ajay explains the etymology of 'I18N' (Internationalization). It originated in computer science because early programmers were lazy typists and shortened the word to 'I' followed by the 18 letters between it and 'N'.

stories.title: Sundar Pichai and the Bangladeshi CEO
stories.description: Ajay recalls a quote from Sundar Pichai: 'It will be a great day for India when a Bangladeshi immigrant becomes the CEO of Infosys.' This parallels Pichai's own success as an Indian immigrant leading Google and highlights the need for true meritocracy.

recommendations.comment: Jagdish Bhagwati's classic book, recommended by Amit.
Research paper by Ajay Shah and others, which forms the basis of this episode's title and theme.

recommendations.item: Kit of Readings on Firm Internationalization
recommendations.comment: Ajay recommends a collection of research papers on the subject instead of a single book.

core_ideas.description: Firms should connect deeply with the global economy through multiple modes: imported inputs, exports, foreign equity (FDI), foreign debt, foreign employees, and outbound FDI. These modes reinforce each other.
The essence of economic development is the creation of high-productivity firms. If 25% of India's population worked in such firms, India would be an advanced economy.
Exporting forces firms to be productive because they cannot manipulate foreign governments like they can the domestic state. It solves the 'toxic domestic political economy' problem.
You cannot pick and choose modes of internationalization. If you want successful exports, you must also accept multinationals, foreign capital, and foreign workers.

core_ideas.item: State's Role: Get Out of the Way
core_ideas.description: The state should stop being hostile to foreign engagement (via agencies like ED, RBI, SEBI) and avoid distorting markets with subsidies (PLI) or exchange rate manipulation.
Amit suggests that 'level of internationalization' is a great heuristic for investors and boards to judge a firm's quality. If a firm is winning globally, it is likely doing things right.

jokes_and_cultural_references.context: Amit jokes about the 'characters' inhabiting Ajay's mind, referring to personifications of economic concepts from previous episodes.

jokes_and_cultural_references.text: I am a podcaster, what do I do?
jokes_and_cultural_references.context: Amit jokingly asks this during the role-playing segment where he asks for advice for different professions.
Ajay uses this term to criticize researchers who are obsessed with Randomized Controlled Trials to the exclusion of broader, more important economic questions.
Amit mocks trivial RCT studies, such as testing if people perceive yellow shirts as brighter than black ones, as a waste of intellect.
